summary: Explains that DES can be broken by brute force by a modestly financed attacker and has been deprecated in favor of AES. It describes risks for applications that still rely on DES. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: DES is a lock with so few possible keys that a determined person can try them all. This note warns that it is no longer safe and that newer locks should be used.

what should i use instead of des
why is des vulnerable to botnets
subtitle: Why DES encryption is no longer safe and what to use instead.

tldr.problem: DES (Data Encryption Standard) has a 56-bit key that is small enough for brute-force attacks using modern hardware, making it unsafe for protecting valuable information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how DES can be cracked using specialized hardware, FPGAs, or botnets, and describes both brute-force attacks and cryptanalytic techniques that break the algorithm in practical timeframes.
tldr.outcome: DES has been deprecated in favor of AES. It should only be used for backward compatibility with legacy systems, not for new applications or high-value data.

today: RFC 4772 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. DES is deprecated by NIST and should not be used for new applications. Use AES for new systems and 3DES only for legacy compatibility.

sections.title: What is DES and Why We Need Better Locks
sections.content:
DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a cipher algorithm the U.S. government approved in the 1970s. It takes a 56-bit key (in practice; the format is 64 bits with 8 parity bits) and encrypts data blocks with it.

For decades, DES was the standard way to protect sensitive data. But in 1998, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) built a specialized machine for less than $250,000 that could crack a DES key in an average of 4.5 days. Since then, computing power and attack methods have improved dramatically.

The core problem: 56 bits sounds large until you realize that brute force requires checking 2^56 (over 72 quadrillion) keys in the worst case. With today's hardware, that is entirely feasible.
sections.eli5: DES is an old code lock that was fine in 1975 but is easy to break now. The key has only 56 bits, which means there are about 72 quadrillion possible combinations, and computers can try them all in less than a day.

sections.title: How DES Gets Broken
sections.content:
There are two main classes of attacks on DES. Brute-force attacks simply try every possible key until the right one is found. In the worst case, this takes 2^56 tries (or 2^55 on average). Even accounting for the work needed to recognize a successful decryption, modern systems can do this in hours.

Cryptanalytic attacks use mathematical properties of the cipher to reduce the search space. The best publicly known attacks (linear and differential cryptanalysis) require 2^43 to 2^47 known plaintext-ciphertext pairs, which is impractical in most cases today. However, even theoretical attacks matter: a 2002 FPGA-based implementation using linear cryptanalysis cracked a DES key in 12-15 hours.

A meet-in-the-middle attack (relevant to 3DES variants) trades computation for storage by precomputing intermediate values, though for plain DES the direct brute-force method is simpler.
sections.eli5: Computers can try billions of key guesses per second. The simplest method—trying every key until one works—takes less than a day. Clever math tricks can do better, proving DES is broken.

sections.title: Real-World Threats: Who Gets Hurt
sections.content:
The RFC identifies high-value targets for DES attacks:

  • Corporate VPNs and remote access connect business offices and employee networks. Attackers targeting industrial espionage have billions of dollars as motivation.
  • Online banking and e-commerce process credit cards and financial transfers. Large banks and merchants are attractive targets for organized crime.
  • Cellular networks and VoIP carry confidential business calls and negotiations.
  • Wireless LANs in financial institutions (like trading floors) are high-value targets.
  • Encrypted laptop hard drives of employees who travel with sensitive data.

In each case, if the window of time that data remains valuable (e.g., a stock trade that executes in minutes) is much longer than the time to crack DES (hours), then DES offers no real protection.
sections.eli5: Banks, companies trading secrets, hospitals, and law enforcement all use encryption. If someone can crack the code in a day, they can steal the secrets before anyone notices.

sections.title: Building a DES Cracker in 2006
sections.content:
The RFC applies Moore's Law—computing power doubles roughly every 18 to 24 months—to estimate DES-cracking costs. A $250,000 dedicated machine in 1998 would cost roughly $15,000 to build in 2006, and a $250,000 investment in 2006 would crack DES in hours instead of days.

FPGAs (Field Programmable Gate Arrays) are flexible chips that can be reprogrammed and cost a fraction of custom silicon (ASICs). A single FPGA can run cryptanalytic attacks, demonstrating that specialized hardware is accessible to skilled attackers.

Botnets present the most dangerous scenario: malicious software (viruses, worms, trojans) that spreads without the owner's knowledge and commandeers millions of computers. Unlike volunteer distributed efforts (like distributed.net in the 1990s), botnets run 24/7 at full capacity. Criminal groups already rent botnets for DDoS attacks; DES-cracking is a natural extension. An attacker needs only a PC to write the malware and access to a botnet—no specialized hardware required.
sections.eli5: In 1998, a DES-cracking machine cost $250,000. Today, computers are faster and cheaper, so the same power costs $15,000 or can be rented from criminals. A hacker can infect millions of computers with a virus to crack keys for free.

sections.title: The Verdict: Don't Use DES
sections.content:
The RFC's recommendation is blunt: DES should not be used for protecting any information that matters. However, three realities slow the transition away from DES:

  • Backward compatibility: Millions of deployed systems still support DES. Replacing all of them is expensive.
  • Performance myths: Many believe DES is faster, but modern PCs handle strong ciphers like AES with no noticeable slowdown. This argument is no longer valid.
  • Ignorance: Some developers do not understand that DES is obsolete.

The RFC suggests: use 3DES (Triple DES) for legacy systems that must maintain backward compatibility, as its 168-bit effective key length resists brute force. Use AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) for new deployments. For legacy code that relies on DES, implement a phased upgrade plan and do not make DES the default cipher.
sections.eli5: The answer is simple: stop using DES. For old systems that need it, use 3DES as a bridge. For anything new, use AES. Don't delay—the longer you use DES, the longer your data is at risk.
